name: Dargwa
confidence_why: Moroz 2019 and Moroz 2015 give Mehweb fixed second-syllable stress, Musaev 1999 and Borise 2018 (after Abdullaev 1954) give the Tsudaqar dialects free contrastive stress, and Moroz 2015 adds that other Dargwa lects stress various syllables, so all sources agree the varieties differ and the only open point is whether literary Akusha Dargwa has weak initial stress (Borise 2018 after Abdullaev 1954) or no clear word stress at all (Musaev 1999).

sweep_summary: darg1241 (North-Central Dargwa) is in the catalog as variable (inter-dialect split: Mehweb fixed second syllable per Moroz 2019; Akusha-Urakhi 'most often initial' carried from Abdullaev 1954 via Borise 2018; Tsudaqar free/phonemic). Two title hits. (1) Xajdakov 1986 'Logical stress and sentence segmentation (Daghestanian data)': sentence-level (focus) prominence, pan-Daghestanian, print-only 1986 Makhachkala volume, no online copy or catalog record found; priority low. (2) Moroz 2014 'Nominal stress in Dargwa languages' (already in our bibliography): the key first-hand cross-dialect survey behind the catalog's split, but no open copy exists — HSE record 136081886 located (page shell saved) yet the publications.hse.ru API could not be reached by automated download on every attempt, and no PDF is exposed anywhere; its content is known only as carried by Borise 2018 (pp. 254, 266: free stress in the Tsudaqar group, second-syllable in Mekege, plural suffixes stress-attracting in some dialects) and by Moroz 2015/2019; consistent with the catalog; priority high. Also read from disk: Moroz 2015 HSE working paper (open; first-hand Mehweb second-syllable rule plus cross-Dargwa remarks, consistent with catalog) and Musaev 1999 in Jazyki mira (scan, scanned, page verified visually): literary Dargwa has no clearly expressed dynamic stress, syllables equal, weak stress sometimes final, no stress minimal pairs, distinct dynamic stress only in Tsudaqar-type dialects — a reachable primary that refines the catalog's carried 'initial stress' claim for Akusha-Urakhi but does not change the variable classification or supersede Moroz 2019 as deciding source. all look-ups went through direct downloads and APIs.

new_statements.quote: 2.1.2. В литературном языке нет четко выраженного динамического ударения. Все слоги в слове произносятся обычно с одинаковой силой. Очень слабое ударение отмечается иногда на последнем слоге. Отсюда – отсутствие случаев словоразличения посредством ударения. Выделяющееся динамическое ударение налицо в диалектах цудахарского типа.
new_statements.translation: 2.1.2. In the literary language there is no clearly expressed dynamic stress. All syllables of a word are usually pronounced with equal force. A very weak stress is sometimes noted on the last syllable. Hence the absence of cases of word-differentiation by means of stress. A distinct dynamic stress is present in the dialects of the Tsudaqar type.
new_statements.citation: Musaev, M.-S.M. 1999. Darginskij jazyk. In M.E. Alekseev, G.A. Klimov, S.A. Starostin & Ja.G. Testelec (eds.), Jazyki mira: Kavkazskie jazyki, 357–368. Moskva: Academia.
new_statements.reading: First-hand statement by a native Dargwa specialist about literary (Akusha-based) Dargwa: no clearly expressed word stress, all syllables roughly equal, at most a very weak stress sometimes on the final syllable, no stress minimal pairs; contrastive dynamic stress exists only in Tsudaqar-type dialects. This refines the catalog's Akusha-Urakhi leg, which currently rests on Borise 2018 carrying Abdullaev 1954 ('fixed, most often on the initial syllable', hedged, secondary only): a reachable primary says the literary variety has weak/absent stress with a final-syllable tendency, not initial stress. It confirms the Tsudaqar free/phonemic stress leg and leaves the languoid-level variable classification (Mehweb fixed second syllable per Moroz 2019 vs Tsudaqar free) intact. Second candidate read this search of works with stress in the title, Moroz 2015 WP BRP 19/LNG/2015 p. 3: 'the northern lects have no geminate and labialized consonants and have fixed stress on the second syllable. Other lects have geminates, labialized consonants and some morphologically governed stress rules (Abdulayev 1954, pp. 23-71)' and p. 7: 'In other Dargwa languages various syllables can be stressed, but there is a strong tendency (a) to stress the second closed syllable of a noun (Ashti, Icari, Khuduc, Qaytagh, Qunqi, Shiri, Tanti) and (b) to have the stress on the verbal root' — first-hand from the author of Moroz 2014, consistent with the catalog.

new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's 'variable' coding and is in fact the primary source behind Borise 2018's second-hand statements (Tsudaqar free stress and Mekegi second-syllable stress cite Moroz 2014: 266 = Table 3/conclusion here; plural morphemes attracting stress cite p. 254). It confirms Mehweb fixed second-syllable stress (p. 257, agreeing with Moroz 2019/2015) and Tsudakhar distinctive, morphologically mobile stress (minimal pairs p. 250; plural, oblique-stem, participle and masdar stress pp. 253-264). It adds detail the catalog lacks: Akusha-Urakhi apparently initial, Mugi/Mekegi second, Mugri final, Gubden stressless; and the explicit morphological stress rules of the central/southern…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress differs across the Dargwa idioms grouped under darg1241. Northern idioms have stress fixed on a particular syllable: Akusha-Urakhi (the base of literary Dargwa) apparently on the first syllable (hedged 'видимо'; the two literary sources Abdullaev 1954 and Sulejmanov 2003 mark the same words initial vs final), Mugi, Mekegi and Mehweb on the second, Mugri on the last, and Gubden is reported to have lost stress. Central and southern idioms (Tsudakhar, Usisha/Butri, Lower Mulebki, Urkarakh, Kharbuk, Tanti, Kubachi, Ashti, Icari, Xuduc, Qunqi, Kajtag, Chirag) have distinctive stress whose position in nouns is governed by morphology and syllable structure: stress moves to the plural suffix (10 idioms incl. Tsudakhar, Usisha), stress shift marks the oblique stem of declension-I nouns (CV́CV absolutive -> CVCV́- oblique; Tsudakhar, Butri, Kharbuk etc.), final-syllable stress forms the short participle (8 idioms incl. Tsudakhar, Butri, Urkarakh), the masdar suffix -ni/-ri is always stressed in central/southern idioms, and in the south two competing tendencies place stress on the last closed syllable of the stem or on the second syllable of 3+-syllable words; Kubachi has stress fixed on the final syllable.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing on secondary stress; the author notes (fn. 2, p. 245) that no detailed acoustic analysis or perception experiments were carried out.
new_statements.exceptions: Tsudakhar vocative retracts stress to the first syllable (tːutːéš 'father' vs hej tːútːeš 'father!', p. 266); derivational suffixes such as -dix attract stress in many idioms except Karbachimakhi (pp. 266-267); nouns derived from masdars shift stress to the first syllable (Tsudakhar dás.ni 'glue' < dasiz, p. 264); lexical exceptions to the closed-syllable rule (Tanti kːúkːuk, Icari šínt'ar, Kajtag jáwsan, májdam, túχum); Shakhbanova 2010's claim of initial stress in Karbachimakhi plurals is contradicted by the author's Xuduc data (p. 255).
new_statements.identity_note: Moroz 2014 treats the whole Dargwa branch (22 idioms). The idioms falling under Glottolog darg1241 (North-Central Dargwa) that it discusses: literary/Akusha, Urakhi, Mugi, Mugri, Lower Mulebki (Akusha-Urakhi dialect), Mekegi, Gubden (Mjurego-Gubden dialect), Mehweb, Tsudakhar, Usisha and its Butri subdialect, and Muira idioms Urkarakh, Tsurai, Kharbuk; its main first-hand data are from southern idioms (Xuduc, Qunqi, Tanti, Ashti, Icari) that Glottolog files under other Dargwa glottocodes. Xajdakov 1986 (not obtained) is a cross-Daghestanian paper on logical (sentence) stress whose Dargwa assignment in Glottolog is computer-generated.

readall_conflicts: No new conflicts: neither listed work could be opened, so nothing was added or contradicted. The conflict already on record stands: the catalog's Akusha-Urakhi leg rests on Borise 2018 carrying Abdullaev 1954 (fixed, most often initial), while the reachable primary Musaev 1999 (existing statement, sect. 2.1.2, p. 359) says literary Dargwa has no clearly expressed dynamic stress with at most a weak final-syllable tendency; Mehweb (Moroz 2019/2015) is fixed second syllable and Tsudaqar dialects have free, phonemic stress. The languoid-level classification variable (inter-dialect divergence) is unchanged. No source contradicts the catalog's dialect-variable picture (Mehweb fixed second-syllable stress; Tsudakhar free/distinctive stress): Moroz 2014 confirms both legs first-hand and is the primary behind Borise 2018's citations. The one unsettled point is the literary/Akusha-Urakhi variety: Moroz 2014 p. 257 says its stress is 'apparently' fixed on the first syllable (following Abdullaev 1954's markings r=úrsi, wárhi, úrč'i), while the same page-248/249 examples show Sulejmanov 2003 marking those words with final stress (r=ursí, warhí, urč'í), and Musaev 1999 (statement held by the project) says literary Dargwa has no clearly expressed dynamic stress, all syllables about equal, at most a very weak stress sometimes on the last syllable. So for the standard variety the sources give initial (Abdullaev 1954 via Moroz, hedged), final (Sulejmanov 2003 markings; Musaev's weak final ten…
